sentence: The NHS calls hormone replacement therapy (HRT) the main medicine for menopause and perimenopause symptoms.
NICE advises offering HRT first for hot flushes and night sweats, after discussing short- and long-term benefits and risks.
Options that do not use hormones include cognitive behavioural therapy, certain medicines for hot flushes, and lubricants for vaginal dryness.
Unscheduled vaginal bleeding should be reported to a GP.
NICE guidance covers hot flushes and night sweats, vaginal and urinary symptoms, and effects on mood.
The perimenopause is the time of change before periods stop, and symptoms can begin then.
note: NHS treatment page covers perimenopause symptoms; definition textbook.

sentence: The NHS lists hot flushes, night sweats, low mood or anxiety, mood swings, brain fog, difficulty sleeping and changes to periods.
Others include palpitations, weakening bones, urinary incontinence, headaches and migraines, joint pains, hair thinning, dry skin and reduced sex drive.
The NHS says a person may have a number of symptoms, or none.
Menopause is confirmed once a person has had no period for 12 months.
The NHS says menopause usually affects people between the ages of 45 and 55, though it can happen earlier, and that the perimenopause can last for a few months or several years.
The NHS says the main medicine for menopause and perimenopause symptoms is hormone replacement therapy, or HRT.
Oestrogen comes as skin patches, a gel or spray, implants or tablets.
Anyone who still has a womb also needs a progestogen to protect the womb lining.
The NHS says a GP will discuss any risks.
According to the NHS, hot flushes or night sweats often improve within a few weeks.
Other symptoms, such as mood changes and vaginal dryness, can take a few months to improve.
The NHS says HRT can lower the risk of osteoporosis, the thinning of the bones.
note: Search summary: HRT can lower risk of osteoporosis and heart disease; heart disease claim dropped pending second pass.

sentence: Some types of HRT can raise the risk of breast cancer, and blood clots are also a recognised risk.
note: Search summary: breast cancer, blood clots.

sentence: Because benefits and risks differ from person to person, the NHS and NICE both describe a discussion with a clinician.
note: NICE: after discussing short- and long-term benefits and risks.

sentence: Low-dose vaginal oestrogen in tablet, cream or ring form can treat vaginal dryness and urinary symptoms.
For people who cannot or choose not to take HRT, the NHS lists CBT for mood, sleep and some physical symptoms, and certain medicines for hot flushes.
Vaginal lubricants and moisturisers are also used.
Regular weight-bearing exercise, cutting down on caffeine, alcohol and spicy food, and stopping smoking can help with hot flushes.
The NHS says to speak to a GP if symptoms are frequent or severe, or if considering HRT.
NICE advises referral to a menopause specialist if treatment does not improve symptoms or causes ongoing side effects.
NICE says unscheduled vaginal bleeding should be reported to a GP.
The NHS also advises a GP appointment for palpitations, for bleeding that is heavier than before while periods continue, and for any vaginal bleeding after periods have stopped for 12 months or more.
Menopause before the age of 40 is called premature menopause or premature ovarian insufficiency, and causes include surgery to remove the ovaries, though sometimes the reason is unknown.
NICE suggests considering HRT for low mood that begins around the same time as other menopause symptoms, when the person does not meet the criteria for depression.
Menopause can affect mood and sleep. If low mood becomes severe or there are thoughts of self-harm, help is open at any time.
